rewritten_text:
Horrified by Sikes’s crime, young Charles Bates began to consider whether an honest life might, after all, be the best one. Deciding that it certainly was, he turned away from his former surroundings, determined to make amends by beginning again elsewhere. For a time he struggled fiercely and suffered considerably, but his contented temperament and good intentions eventually brought success. After working as a farmer’s laborer and a carrier’s boy, he has become the happiest young cattle farmer in all Northamptonshire.

And now the hand writing these words hesitates as its work approaches its end, wishing to weave the thread of these adventures just a little longer.

I would gladly stay awhile with some of those whose company I have kept so long, and share their happiness by trying to describe it. I would show Rose Maylie in the full beauty and grace of early womanhood, casting a gentle light along her quiet path through life, a light that touched everyone walking beside her and reached into their hearts. I would portray her as the life and joy of gatherings by the fireside and cheerful summer parties. I would follow her across the hot fields at noon and listen to her soft, sweet voice on moonlit evening walks. I would watch her goodness and generosity outside her home, and the smiling, tireless way she fulfilled her household duties within it. I would picture her and her dead sister’s child rejoicing in their love for each other, spending whole hours imagining the friends they had so sorrowfully lost. Once again I would call to mind those happy little faces gathered around her knee and hear their merry chatter. I would recall the sound of her clear laugh and summon the tear of sympathy shining in her gentle blue eye. These things, and a thousand expressions, smiles, turns of thought, and ways of speaking—I would gladly bring back every one.

How Mr. Brownlow continued, day after day, to fill his adopted child’s mind with knowledge, loving him more deeply as his character unfolded and revealed the flourishing beginnings of everything he hoped the boy would become; how he discovered fresh traces of his early friend in him, stirring old memories that were sad but also sweet and comforting; how the two orphans, tested by hardship, remembered its lessons through compassion toward others, love for one another, and heartfelt gratitude to Him who had guarded and preserved them—all these things need no further telling.

“If I can't manage to live on that, I won't ask anyone to lend me a hand. Is that satisfactory?”

A tremendous roar of applause arose, and through it came the king’s voice:

“Strike off his bonds and give him freedom! Let all pay him homage, the high and low, the wealthy and the poor, for he has become the king’s right hand, invested with authority and power, and shall sit upon the throne’s highest step! Now banish this advancing night and restore the light and gladness, so that the whole world may bless thee.”

But I answered:

“It matters little if a common man is put to shame before the world; but the king would be dishonored if those who saw his minister naked did not also behold him freed from that shame. If I might request the return of my clothes—”

“They are unsuitable,” the king interrupted. “Bring garments of a different kind. Dress him as a prince!”

My plan succeeded. I wanted matters to remain as they were until the eclipse became total; otherwise they would again press me to send away the darkness, which of course I could not do. Fetching the clothes bought some time, though not enough. I therefore needed a further excuse. I explained that it would be quite natural for the king to reconsider and regret, to some degree, what he had done in his excitement. Accordingly, I would allow the darkness to deepen awhile; if, after a reasonable interval, his intentions remained unchanged, I would dismiss it. Neither the king nor anyone else liked that proposal, but I had to hold my ground.

As I wrestled with those clumsy sixth-century garments, the darkness grew deeper and blacker. Finally it was pitch dark. The crowd groaned in terror as cold, eerie night breezes swept through the place and stars emerged, twinkling overhead. At last the eclipse was complete, much to my relief, though everyone else was miserable, naturally enough. I declared:

“By remaining silent, the king continues to accept the terms.” Then I raised my hands, held that posture for a moment, and pronounced with the most dreadful solemnity: “Let this enchantment melt away and depart without harm!”

For a moment there was no answer in the profound darkness and the silence of a graveyard. Then, a moment or two later, the sun’s silver edge thrust into view. The gathering erupted in a mighty shout and poured toward me like a flood, overwhelming me with gratitude and blessings. Clarence was certainly not among the last carried in by the tide.

In this manner two years went by. Day followed day, hundreds of them passing without any outward alteration, though a few changes slowly took place within my mind as I drifted toward death. I applied myself more to study, entered more fully into the thoughts others had set down in books, read history, and lost my separate identity among the multitude who had lived before me. Perhaps, as the feeling of immediate anguish faded, I grew more human. Solitude, too, surrendered some of its attractions. Once more I longed for sympathy, not that I was ever drawn to seek the crowd, but I wanted a single friend who would love me. Perhaps you will say that I was gradually becoming ready to return to society. I cannot think so. The sympathy I craved had to be so pure, so free from the influence of external circumstances, that in the world I could only have been frustrated by the coarse elements forever mingling with even its finest feelings. Believe me, I was then less suited than before to any fellowship with my fellow creatures. When I withdrew from them, they had troubled me as pain or illness troubles one: something outside the mind that chafed it and that I wished to throw off. But now I would have sought sympathy, desired to bind my soul to another’s, and thus prepared abundant draughts of disappointment and sorrow for myself. I was as delicate as the sensitive plant, all nerves. I wanted neither sympathy nor assistance in ambition or learning, but gentle, reciprocal affection: encouraging smiles and tender words of consolation. I longed for one heart into which I might freely pour my complaints, so that the heavenly quality of its soil could bring forth blessed fruit from such poor seed. Yet where could I find it? Love, the soul of friendship, is a gentle spirit rarely discovered except where two kindly beings have been joined since youth, or united by shared suffering and endeavors. To certain chosen people it comes unexpectedly and unsought, falling like soft dew upon favored places which, however barren before, grow fertile in every lovely plant beneath its gracious influence. But pursuit makes it flee; it mocks the prayers of its worshippers. It will give itself, but will not be sought.

Knowing all this, I did not go in search of sympathy. Yet there upon my lonely heath, beneath my humble roof, with wilderness surrounding me, it came like a winter sunbeam, beautifying the drifted snow even as it helps to melt it. Alas, that sunlight fell on blighted fruit. Its brightness did not revive me, for I was too utterly ruined to feel its gentle strength.
